2	
3	\paragraph{Expert budget threshold.}
4	EC-HTE requires at least $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for the hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage estimates to stabilize.
5	Below this threshold, per-subgroup confusion matrix estimates are too noisy for reliable inversion, and stratified MLE is preferred.
6	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics, making the hierarchical model unnecessary at large expert budgets.
7	
8	\paragraph{RMSE tradeoff at small $n$.}
9	EC-HTE achieves lower bias than global correction but incurs higher variance when the expert budget is small relative to the number of subgroups.
10	In the most unfavorable configuration ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$), EC-HTE CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
11	Practitioners should weigh whether bias or variance is more consequential for their application before adopting subgroup-stratified correction at small sample sizes.
12	
13	\paragraph{Plug-in standard errors.}
14	The variance-adjusted CausalForest propagates outcome uncertainty through the inverse confusion matrix $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ but does not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.

\section{Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection}
\label{app:hatespeech}

We apply EC-HTE to the UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus~\cite{kennedy2020constructing}, annotating 2{,}496 comments for dehumanization using GPT-4.1.
Four text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing platform (Reddit/Gab vs.\ Twitter/YouTube) and text length (above/below median), yielding balanced groups ($n \approx 624$ each).
Per-subgroup misclassification rates range from 0.266 to 0.383, confirming heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.117$) in a real annotation setting.

CATE correction results are mixed: EC-HTE does not improve over global correction, and both corrected estimators produce wider confidence intervals than the naive baseline.
The underlying cause is a global FNR of 53\%, which renders the confusion matrices near-singular (condition numbers $> 50$).
Under such extreme baseline error, matrix inversion amplifies noise regardless of stratification strategy.
This case study confirms that subgroup-varying misclassification rates are not an artifact of synthetic design but arise naturally in real NLP annotation tasks.
The high baseline FNR illustrates a boundary condition: when overall misclassification is extreme, EC-HTE's bias reduction is overwhelmed by variance from near-singular inversion, and practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying correction.

\section{Cross-Model Consistency}
\label{app:multilm}

We evaluate whether misclassification heterogeneity is model-specific by annotating 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with six OpenAI models spanning three generations.
Small subgroups ($n < 10$) are excluded; effective $\Delta\pi$ is computed over the four retained text-feature subgroups.

\label{tab:multilm}

All six models exhibit $\Delta\pi > 0.05$ (Table~\ref{tab:multilm}), and 5 of 6 share the same worst subgroup (\texttt{True\_medium}: tweets with hashtags and medium text length).
Spearman rank correlations of per-subgroup error rates between model pairs range from $\rho = 0.80$ to $1.00$, indicating that the subgroup error structure is consistent across architectures.
Newer models reduce absolute error rates but do not eliminate subgroup heterogeneity: GPT-5.4 achieves $\Delta\pi = 0.114$ compared to GPT-3.5-Turbo's $0.198$.
These results were obtained with a single API provider; cross-provider validation is left to future work.

\section{Robustness to Subgroup Misspecification}
\label{app:robustness}

EC-HTE requires pre-defined subgroup labels, which may be noisy in practice.
We test robustness by randomly flipping each observation's subgroup assignment with probability $p_{\text{flip}} \in \{0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50\}$, across $K \in \{2, 4\}$ (extreme regime, $n_{\text{expert}} = 500$, $\Delta\tau = 0.3$, 100 MC runs).

\begin{table}[t]

EC-HTE maintains coverage $\geq 0.945$ across all configurations (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}), while the naive estimator is systematically below nominal (0.875--0.919).
At $p_{\text{flip}} = 0.50$, subgroup structure is effectively destroyed; EC-HTE converges to global correction (coverage and RMSE within 0.1\%), confirming that hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage provides a built-in safety mechanism.
For $K{=}4$ at $p_{\text{flip}} = 0.50$, a small residual RMSE gap persists ($p < 0.01$), reflecting the variance cost of estimating four confusion matrices even when they carry no signal.

The high baseline FNR illustrates a boundary condition: when overall misclassification is extreme, EC-HTE's bias reduction is overwhelmed by variance from near-singular inversion, and practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying correction.
